# Introduction

<!-- Background and motivation for the study -->

The vast majority of phenotypic descriptions in the scientific literature are expressed using natural language, including the comparative character matrices used in evolutionary systematic studies. The [Phenoscape project](https://kb.phenoscape.org/) spearheaded the application of structured, formal annotations to these datasets using biomedical ontologies, facilitating integration and semantic query across multiple studies in a common knowledgebase.

[Dahdul et al. (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1093/database/bay110) analyzed annotation consistency across human curators and compared the performance of an automated NLP tool—*Semantic CharaParser*—against a Gold Standard dataset using ontology-based semantic similarity metrics.

# Evolutionary Character States

<div style="float: left; width: 45%; margin: 0 1em 0.5em 0;">
```{r chakrabarty-fig, fig.cap="Examples of morphological characters and states from Chakrabarty (2007).", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("chakrabarty-characters.png")
```
</div>

In comparative morphology, organisms are described using **characters** (observable anatomical features) and **states** (the specific forms a character takes across taxa). For example, a character might be "shape of the caudal fin" with states such as "forked" or "rounded." Character–state matrices underpin phylogenetic analyses of morphological change.

Phenoscape annotates character states with ontology terms using an Entity–Quality (EQ) model, enabling compatibility with model organism databases describing developmental phenotypes, linking free-text morphological observations to formal knowledge representations.

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

# Original Methodology

**Human Curators.** Three curators (WD, AD, NI) each EQ-annotated the same set of characters in two rounds, using the Phenex annotation software: a Naive Round (NR, working with only the character–state text) and a subsequent Knowledge Round (KR, with full access to the source publication and other literature).

**Automated Annotations.** Semantic CharaParser was used to generate automated annotations from the same character descriptions.

## Groupwise Semantic Similarity

Because annotations reference ontology terms, comparison between two annotations is not binary (match/no-match) but graded: terms that share more ontological ancestors are more semantically similar than terms that share fewer. We use two complementary similarity measures computed over ontology-derived ancestor sets.

**Jaccard Similarity (SimJ).** For each pair of annotation classes, we compute the full set of ontological ancestors (superclasses via the ELK reasoner over a merged ontology of UBERON, PATO, BSPO, and GO, enriched with expressions materializing additional axes of classification based on relations, e.g., *part_of*). SimJ is the ratio of shared ancestors to total ancestors:

$$\text{SimJ}(A, B) = \frac{|Anc(A) \cap Anc(B)|}{|Anc(A) \cup Anc(B)|}$$

SimJ ranges from 0 (no shared ancestry) to 1 (identical ancestor sets). For each character-state, we take the maximum SimJ across all EQ pairings between the two annotation sets, capturing the best-case alignment.

**Normalized Information Content (NIC).** While SimJ treats all ancestors equally, NIC weights them by specificity. The Information Content of a term reflects how rarely it appears as an ancestor across the corpus: $IC(t) = -\log_2 \frac{freq(t)}{N}$. For each class pair, we identify the Most Informative Common Ancestor (MICA) and normalize:

$$\text{NIC}(A, B) = \frac{IC(\text{MICA}(A, B))}{IC_{\max}}$$

NIC complements SimJ by giving higher scores when two annotations share a specific, informative common ancestor rather than only broad, general ones.

## Partial Precision and Recall

A single character-state may be annotated with multiple EQ statements. To compare annotation sets of different sizes, we adapt precision and recall using best-match averaging over pairwise SimJ scores.

**Partial Precision** measures how well each curator/agent EQ is represented in the Gold Standard. For each EQ in the test annotation, we find its best SimJ match among the GS EQs and average:

$$PP = \frac{1}{|C|} \sum_{c \in C} \max_{g \in GS} \text{SimJ}(c, g)$$

**Partial Recall** measures how well each Gold Standard EQ is captured by the test annotation. For each EQ in the GS, we find its best SimJ match among the test EQs:

$$PR = \frac{1}{|GS|} \sum_{g \in GS} \max_{c \in C} \text{SimJ}(g, c)$$

High precision with low recall indicates the annotator produced correct but incomplete annotations; high recall with low precision suggests over-annotation or imprecise term selection.

# Extending with Agentic Annotation

<!-- Describe the AI agent annotation approach and how it parallels the original study design -->

We extend the original study by introducing AI agent annotators (Claude 4.6 and GPT 5.4) as additional participants, evaluated using the same metrics and Gold Standard. Like the human curators, the AI agents annotated in two rounds, enabling direct comparison across all annotator types.

## Agent Workspace

Each AI agent is launched within a self-contained workspace:

```
ai-annotation/
├── input/
│   ├── characters/         ← per-character TSVs
│   ├── papers/             ← source publication PDFs
│   ├── ontologies/         ← UBERON, PATO, BSPO, GO
│   └── annotation_guide.md
├── output/                 ← agent annotation results
├── scripts/
│   └── validate_annotations.scala
└── .claude/
    └── skills/
        └── phenotype-eq-annotation/
            └── SKILL.md
```

# Results

```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)

datadir <- "../data/CombinedComparisons"

# Helper: load one annotator's scores vs GS into a data frame
load_scores <- function(label, type, sim_file, pp_file, pr_file) {
  sim <- read.table(file.path(datadir, sim_file), header = TRUE, sep = "\t")
  pp  <- read.table(file.path(datadir, pp_file),  header = TRUE, sep = "\t")
  pr  <- read.table(file.path(datadir, pr_file),  header = TRUE, sep = "\t")
  data.frame(
    Annotator = label,
    Type = type,
    CharNum = sim$Character.Number,
    SimJ = sim$SimJ.Score,
    NIC  = sim$NIC.Score,
    PP   = pp$SimJ.Partial.Precision,
    PR   = pr$SimJ.Partial.Recall
  )
}

# ---- Human curators vs GS ----
scores <- rbind(
  load_scores("WD",  "Human", "KR--WD_40717--GS_Dataset.tsv",  "PP_KR--WD_40717--GS_Dataset.tsv",  "PR_KR--WD_40717--GS_Dataset.tsv"),
  load_scores("AD",  "Human", "KR--AD_40718--GS_Dataset.tsv",  "PP_KR--AD_40718--GS_Dataset.tsv",  "PR_KR--AD_40718--GS_Dataset.tsv"),
  load_scores("NI",  "Human", "KR--NI_40716--GS_Dataset.tsv",  "PP_KR--NI_40716--GS_Dataset.tsv",  "PR_KR--NI_40716--GS_Dataset.tsv"),

  # ---- SCP (CharaParser) vs GS ----
  load_scores("SCP Best",      "SCP",   "Transformed_CP_best--GS_Dataset.tsv", "PP_Transformed_CP_best--GS_Dataset.tsv", "PR_Transformed_CP_best--GS_Dataset.tsv"),

  # ---- AI agents vs GS ----
  load_scores("Claude Opus 4.6 (high)",      "AI",  "AI--Claude_46_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv",  "PP_AI--Claude_46_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv",  "PR_AI--Claude_46_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv"),
  load_scores("Claude Sonnet 4.6 (medium)", "AI",  "AI--Sonnet_46--GS_Dataset.tsv",     "PP_AI--Sonnet_46--GS_Dataset.tsv",     "PR_AI--Sonnet_46--GS_Dataset.tsv"),
  load_scores("GPT 5.4 (xhigh)",            "AI",  "AI--GPT_54_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv",     "PP_AI--GPT_54_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv",     "PR_AI--GPT_54_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv"),
  load_scores("GPT 5.4 Mini (high)",        "AI",  "AI--GPT_54_Mini--GS_Dataset.tsv",   "PP_AI--GPT_54_Mini--GS_Dataset.tsv",   "PR_AI--GPT_54_Mini--GS_Dataset.tsv")
  # ---- Add new agent curators here ----
)

library(plyr)

# ---- R1 vs R2 comparison data (all characters) ----
r1r2_scores <- rbind(
  load_scores("Claude Opus 4.6 R1", "R1", "AI--Claude_46--GS_Dataset.tsv",    "PP_AI--Claude_46--GS_Dataset.tsv",    "PR_AI--Claude_46--GS_Dataset.tsv"),
  load_scores("Claude Opus 4.6 R2", "R2", "AI--Claude_46_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv", "PP_AI--Claude_46_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv", "PR_AI--Claude_46_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv"),
  load_scores("GPT 5.4 R1",         "R1", "AI--GPT_54--GS_Dataset.tsv",       "PP_AI--GPT_54--GS_Dataset.tsv",       "PR_AI--GPT_54--GS_Dataset.tsv"),
  load_scores("GPT 5.4 R2",         "R2", "AI--GPT_54_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv",    "PP_AI--GPT_54_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv",    "PR_AI--GPT_54_R2--GS_Dataset.tsv")
)
r1r2_long <- melt(r1r2_scores[, !(names(r1r2_scores) %in% "CharNum")],
                   id.vars = c("Annotator", "Type"),
                   variable.name = "Metric", value.name = "Score")
r1r2_summary <- ddply(r1r2_long, .(Annotator, Type, Metric), summarise,
                      Mean = mean(Score, na.rm = TRUE),
                      SE   = sd(Score, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(Score))),
                      Lower = Mean - 1.96 * SE,
                      Upper = Mean + 1.96 * SE)
r1r2_order <- c("Claude Opus 4.6 R1", "Claude Opus 4.6 R2",
                "GPT 5.4 R1", "GPT 5.4 R2")
r1r2_summary$Annotator <- factor(r1r2_summary$Annotator, levels = rev(r1r2_order))

# ---- Main figure data (characters 51–203 only) ----
scores_filtered <- scores[scores$CharNum > 50, ]

scores_long <- melt(scores_filtered[, !(names(scores_filtered) %in% "CharNum")],
                    id.vars = c("Annotator", "Type"),
                    variable.name = "Metric", value.name = "Score")

# Compute mean and 95% CI per annotator per metric
score_summary <- ddply(scores_long, .(Annotator, Type, Metric), summarise,
                       Mean = mean(Score, na.rm = TRUE),
                       SE   = sd(Score, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(Score))),
                       Lower = Mean - 1.96 * SE,
                       Upper = Mean + 1.96 * SE)

# Order annotators logically
annotator_order <- c(
  "WD", "AD", "NI",
  "SCP Best",
  "Claude Opus 4.6 (high)",
  "Claude Sonnet 4.6 (medium)",
  "GPT 5.4 (xhigh)",
  "GPT 5.4 Mini (high)"
)
score_summary$Annotator <- factor(score_summary$Annotator, levels = rev(annotator_order))

# Compute human curator mean and SD per metric for reference band
human_means <- ddply(score_summary[score_summary$Type == "Human", ], .(Metric), summarise,
                     HumanMean = mean(Mean),
                     HumanSD = sd(Mean),
                     HumanLower = mean(Mean) - sd(Mean),
                     HumanUpper = mean(Mean) + sd(Mean))
```

```{r r1r2-figure, fig.cap="Improvement from Round 1 to Round 2 (all 203 characters). Instructions were refined after reviewing the first 50 characters.", fig.height=3.5, fig.width=10}
ggplot(r1r2_summary, aes(x = Mean, y = Annotator, color = Type, shape = Type)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = Lower, xmax = Upper), height = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Metric, nrow = 1, strip.position = "top") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("R1" = "grey50", "R2" = "#2980b9")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1), labels = c("0", "", "0.5", "", "1"),
                     limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Score", y = NULL, color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "italic", size = 14),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1.0, "lines")
  )
```

```{r results-figure, fig.cap="Mean similarity scores (with 95% CI) for each annotator vs. the Gold Standard (characters 51–203 only). Shaded band shows human curator mean ± 1 SD.", fig.height=7, fig.width=10}
ggplot(score_summary, aes(x = Mean, y = Annotator, color = Type, shape = Type)) +
  geom_rect(data = human_means,
            aes(xmin = HumanLower, xmax = HumanUpper, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey70", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(data = human_means, aes(xintercept = HumanMean),
             linetype = "solid", color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = Lower, xmax = Upper), height = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Metric, nrow = 1, strip.position = "top") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Human" = "#2c3e50", "SCP" = "#e67e22", "AI" = "#2980b9")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1), labels = c("0", "", "0.5", "", "1"),
                     limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Score", y = NULL, color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "italic", size = 14),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1.0, "lines")
  )
```
